August 2035. Mrs Winter from the publisher has brought the galley proofs of Ludwig's book. Ludwig, Elif and Mrs Winter are reading in the Leseecke (reading corner).
Mr Brandt, these are the galley proofs. Three hundred and twelve pages. I only have a few comments. Most of them are about the connection between the paragraphs.

Nothing serious. Here, for example: “Hotte was an instructor. Hotte was strict. Hotte was also funny.” Hotte three times. You could write: “Hotte was an instructor, although he wasn't only strict but also funny.”
Hm. Still, that doesn't sound like me any more. I'm a tram driver, not a teacher.
Maybe like this: “Hotte was an instructor. He was strict, but at the same time funny.” That sounds like you.
That's good. We'll take that. And here: “Ingrid and Grete were friends. Grete played the piano, Ingrid read.” You don't immediately know who's who.
Yes, you do. Everyone knows who Ingrid is.
Your readers in Munich don't. Maybe: “The former played the piano, the latter read.”
Wait. Then it's not right. Ingrid comes first, so Ingrid is “the former”. But Ingrid didn't play the piano, Grete did. It has to be the other way round.
You're right. So my suggestion is wrong. Ten years old and cleverer than the editor.
Then we'll leave it as it was and write the names. This isn't a book for teachers. Quite the opposite.

The galley proofs arrived on a hot Tuesday in August, in a big brown box that Mrs Winter brought from Kreuzberg herself, by bike, because, as she said, she never entrusts manuscripts to the post. This had been an old rule of her father's, who had founded the publishing house in nineteen seventy-four, and she had never broken it. The box was heavy. Inside were three hundred and twelve loose pages with wide white margins that left room for corrections, and on top a red pencil, just one, carefully sharpened.

“You have three weeks,” said Mrs Winter. “Read everything. Every word. If you want to change something, write it in the margin. If not, don't write anything. After that nothing can be changed, because after that the book goes to the printer's.” Ludwig nodded seriously. He took the red pencil in his hand like a tool he had known for a long time, even though he had never seen a galley proof in his whole life. Then he said something Mrs Winter hadn't expected: “I'm not reading this on my own. I'm too old for that and my arms are too short.”

So for three weeks the Leseecke in the basement of number thirty-three became an editorial office. Every afternoon at four, three people sat there at the old wooden table, under the lamp Andrei had put up four years earlier: Ludwig, who read the pages aloud, slowly, with his reading glasses, which he now wore, though only when no strangers were watching; Elif, who read along and held the red pencil, because Ludwig's hand shook when he wrote; and Katrin Krüger, who came after work at the newspaper and, with thirty years of experience, found every mistake hiding anywhere. The latter brought biscuits every day. The former ate them. Elif wrote.

It was slow work. And yet it wasn't the spelling that caused problems, because Mrs Winter had already had the texts corrected twice, but rather the connection between them. Ludwig had written the stories over five years, in notebooks, on slips of paper, on the backs of till receipts from the café, and some of them repeated each other. The story of Ingrid's Leseecke appeared twice in the book, once on page forty and once on page two hundred and eighty, and the two versions contradicted each other on one point: in the first it had rained during the storm, in the second it had snowed.

“So which was it in the end?” Katrin asked. “Rain or snow?” Ludwig thought for a long time. “It was October,” he said at last. “Consequently it was rain. Admittedly, very cold rain. Almost snow. I think in the second version I wanted to make it more dramatic.” Katrin laughed. “All authors do that,” she said. “The more often they tell a story, the more snow falls in it.” Elif crossed out the second version with the red pencil, neatly, with a single long line, and wrote in the margin: “See page 40.” So the book had one story fewer. And that, Katrin said, was exactly the problem.

In the second week Elif got strict. She had learned from Katrin what to watch out for, and now she watched out for everything. When Ludwig wrote “and then” three times in one paragraph, she drew three little circles in the margin with the red pencil and looked at him expectantly until he sighed and found something else: “after that”, “thereupon”, “shortly afterwards”, “at the same moment”. When he repeated a name too often, she wrote next to it “he?” or “the latter?”. And when two sentences stood side by side with no connection, she drew a little bridge between them, a sign she had invented, which meant: a linking word is missing here. Katrin thought it was so good that she introduced it in her own newsroom the next day. “Elif's bridge”, she called it. Ludwig called it something else. “Elif's bridge,” he said, “is the reason I dream about conjunctions at night.”

The table of contents had, in fact, exactly fifty-two stories. Ludwig had insisted on that. Fifty-two, like the birds Andrei's grandfather had started and Andrei had finished. He had argued about it with Mrs Winter for a whole hour, because the latter had originally wanted only forty stories, because of the costs. Ludwig had won. And now, after Elif's line, there were only fifty-one. “Then one's missing,” said Elif. “We have to find a new one. By Friday.” Ludwig looked at her over the rim of his glasses. “And which one?” he asked. “I've written down everything I know.”

The answer came the next day, and from someone nobody expected. It was Thursday, and on Thursdays Hotte came. He came down the basement stairs, which at ninety was an achievement he was very proud of, and sat down on the chair next to Elif without asking. Then for half an hour he listened to the three of them discussing commas and paragraphs and said nothing, which was so unusual for Hotte that Katrin asked him twice whether he was feeling unwell. Finally he cleared his throat. “I've got a question,” he said. “Does it say in there how you found your Ingrid again?”

The basement went quiet. Ludwig put down the page he was reading. Elif leafed through the table of contents, slowly, from top to bottom, and then once more. “No,” she said at last, surprised. “That isn't anywhere. There's the story about the rock concert, where Ingrid was sitting right at the back reading a book and you didn't ask her name. There's one about the wedding. But something's missing in between. How did you find her again?” Ludwig took off his glasses and rubbed his eyes. “I never wrote that down,” he said quietly. “I thought nobody would be interested. It was just a perfectly ordinary day.”

“Ordinary,” Hotte snorted. “I was there. It wasn't ordinary. It was the daftest day in the history of Berlin public transport.” And then he told the story himself, in Berlin dialect, and Katrin took it down as fast as she could, in shorthand, and Elif translated the hard words for her into standard German, quietly, just mouthing them. It was March nineteen sixty-nine, a week after the concert. Ludwig was twenty, had been a tram driver for a year and had spent the whole week thinking about the girl with the book, without knowing how to find her. He was driving the line that had a different number back then, through Prenzlauer Berg. At one stop a young woman got on, with a pile of books in her arms so high that she couldn't see over it. And when the tram set off, the books fell.

“All of them,” said Hotte. “Twelve books. All over the carriage. And this Ludwig, the most punctual tram driver in the GDR, stops the tram. In the middle of the route. Gets out of his cab. And picks up the books with her. Five minutes. Behind him there are three trams ringing their bells like mad. And I'm in the third one, as an instructor, with a trainee, and I think: what's that lad doing? He's going to lose his job.” Hotte laughed. “He didn't lose it. He got a warning. And a wife.” Ludwig sat completely still. Then he said, without looking up: “I only recognised her when she came out from behind the books. It was the girl from the concert. She was studying to become a teacher. The last book I picked up was the very book she'd been reading at the concert. I said: Is it still better than the music? At that she laughed and said: Because you found me, I'll lend it to you.”

Ludwig wrote the new story in a single night, in his kitchen, by hand, on six pages of an old school exercise book. He wrote it in standard German, but he left three of Hotte's sentences in Berlin dialect, exactly as Hotte had said them, because, as he explained to Mrs Winter the next morning, otherwise they wouldn't be true. Mrs Winter read the six pages at a table in the café while her coffee went cold. Then she put them down and said nothing. Then she said: “This is the first story in the book. Not the fifty-second. The first.” Ludwig wanted to argue. But he couldn't think of a single argument. Quite the opposite: he realised she was right. So the book was complete, with fifty-two stories, and the table of contents had to be changed one last time.

He wrote until shortly after three in the morning. At half past three, Lena, who got up early because of the bakery, saw a light in his kitchen and knocked on the door. Ludwig was sitting at the table, with the exercise book in front of him, next to it a cup of cold tea and the old photo of Ingrid at twenty-one that usually hung in the hallway. He had taken it down and put it in front of him, like a witness. “I wanted to be sure I wasn't telling anything wrong,” he told Lena when she asked. “She'd have corrected me. She always corrected me. Especially the commas.” Lena read the six pages standing up, in her baker's apron, and when she had finished she just said: “Grandad, a bridge is missing on page three.” Ludwig laughed so loudly that on the first floor, at Andrei's, the light went on.

On Friday evening, when Mrs Winter had left with the brown box on her bike rack, Ludwig, Elif and Hotte stayed out in the courtyard for a while, under the chestnut tree. The first leaves were already turning yellow, although it was still August. Ludwig had kept the red pencil. Mrs Winter had said he could keep it as a memento, that it was a tradition at the publishing house. He turned it between his fingers. “You know, Hotte,” he said at last, “for sixty-six years I thought nobody but me remembered that day.” Hotte shrugged. “That's the trouble with you writers,” he said. “You think you're the only ones who listen.”
